opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a lot of potential there, though I'd say it's less "replace" in a single jump and more a gradual shift as we solve some of the practical problems.

The motivation is pretty compelling. Subword tokenizers like BPE are a kind of frozen preprocessing step that sits outside the model. They're learned once from some corpus, and then everything downstream inherits their quirks. You see it in how models struggle with character-level tasks like spelling, counting letters, or handling typos. You see it in multilingual settings too: languages that are underrepresented in the tokenizer's training data get split into many more tokens. So those speakers effectively pay more in compute and context length, and the model often does worse on those languages. Bytes give you a universal, lossless interface. Any text in any script maps onto the same 256 symbols, and nothing is out of vocabulary.

The big obstacle has always been efficiency. Byte sequences are several times longer than subword sequences, and with attention scaling the way it does, that's very expensive in both training and inference. That's what a lot of my work has focused on. With MrT5, for example, the idea was to keep the byte-level input but let the model learn to dynamically delete or merge tokens in its early layers. The model decides for itself which information it can compress, rather than relying on a fixed tokenizer to make that decision up front. We found we could cut sequence length substantially while keeping performance close to the full byte-level model.

More broadly, I think the direction the field is heading is learned, dynamic segmentation inside the model, whether through deletion, pooling, patching based on entropy, or hierarchical architectures. In a sense, tokenization doesn't disappear. It becomes something the model learns end to end rather than a hand-designed preprocessing step.

So will bytes fully replace subwords? I'm optimistic, but there are real challenges left. Inference speed matters a lot for deployment, and an enormous amount of infrastructure and engineering has been built around subword models. Byte-level and dynamically compressed models need to be clearly better, or at least matched on efficiency, before people switch at scale. But the benefits for robustness, multilinguality, and simply removing a brittle component from the pipeline are real. I'd be surprised if, a few years from now, the dominant models still relied on a static BPE vocabulary the way they do today.

r001.rationale: The response says byte-level models can dynamically delete or merge tokens to compress sequences, but it does not say this targets highly predictable sequences or that it yields fewer processing units than subword models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that I don't view byte-level modeling as something that's going to fully replace tokenization overnight, but I do think it has a real shot at becoming the default for a lot of use cases, and the reason I'm excited about it is that tokenization is kind of this weird vestigial piece of the pipeline. It's a separate preprocessing step that's trained with its own objective, usually something like BPE, that's totally disconnected from the language modeling objective. And it has all these downstream consequences that people have documented pretty well at this point. You get these inefficiencies and unfairness across languages, where English gets a very compact tokenization and other languages, especially ones that aren't well represented in the tokenizer training data, get fragmented into way more tokens. So those languages are more expensive to process and often modeled worse. You get brittleness to things like typos or unusual spellings, because a single character change can completely change the token sequence. And you get these kind of famous failure modes around things like counting letters in a word or doing arithmetic, which are really just artifacts of the model never seeing the characters.

So the appeal of going to bytes is that you get rid of all of that. The vocabulary is tiny, it's universal across languages and scripts, and the model gets to learn whatever internal representation of the input it actually needs rather than having that decided for it in advance. The obvious problem, and this is the thing that's kept byte-level models from taking over, is that sequences get much longer. You're looking at something like four or five times as many units for English text compared to a typical subword tokenizer, and worse for some other languages, and attention costs scale with sequence length, so naively that's a big compute hit.

The way I think about it, and the way a lot of the recent work has gone, is that the right move is not to throw out the idea of operating on larger chunks, it's to make the chunking learned and dynamic instead of fixed and static. So in my own work, MrT5, which builds on ByteT5, the idea was to add a learned gating mechanism in the encoder that decides which byte-level positions to keep and which ones to drop after a few layers, so the model essentially learns its own compression. And what you find is that the model learns to drop a lot of tokens, sometimes fifty percent or more, with very little loss in quality, and importantly, it adapts the compression rate to the input. That's something a fixed tokenizer fundamentally can't do. And then you've got other work in the same spirit, things like Byte Latent Transformer from Meta or the hierarchical approaches, where you have a small byte-level model that patches things up into latent units for a bigger model to operate on. Those all share this philosophy of, let's keep bytes as the interface to the world, but let the model figure out the granularity.

So to directly answer the question, I'd say the potential is high, but the path there runs through these kinds of adaptive or hierarchical architectures rather than through pure flat byte-level transformers. The remaining open questions for me are mostly about scale, whether these approaches hold up or even improve at frontier model sizes where the training budgets are enormous, and about the whole ecosystem being built around tokens, like everything from serving infrastructure to pricing is per-token. There's a lot of inertia there. But I think that if you look at the trajectory, tokenization is one of the last hand-designed pieces of the pipeline, and historically those tend to get replaced by learned components eventually.

r001.rationale: The response describes learned byte-position dropping and adaptive compression, including dropping 50% or more with little quality loss. It does not say compression targets highly predictable sequences or that the resulting sequences use fewer processing units than subword tokenization.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a really promising direction. With subword tokenization, you’re introducing a fixed vocabulary that determines how text gets broken up before the model ever sees it. And those choices can work much better for some languages than for others. Byte-level modeling gives you a more general representation without having to design that vocabulary upfront.

The big trade-off is sequence length. If you represent everything as bytes, the model has to process many more positions, and that can get expensive. So the question is whether we can build architectures that learn to group bytes into useful representations while keeping the computation manageable.

I wouldn’t say it’s inevitable that byte-level models will replace subword models, but I think there’s a compelling case for exploring them. You’re letting the model learn more of the structure itself, rather than baking that structure into the tokenizer.

r001.rationale: The response mentions grouping bytes to manage computation, but does not say downsampling compresses highly predictable sequences into fewer processing units than subword models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a really interesting direction. With subword tokenization, you’re making decisions about how to segment language before the model ever sees it, and those decisions don’t necessarily work equally well across languages. Going down to bytes gives you a much more general representation and lets the model learn how to compose those units.

The big challenge is efficiency. The same text becomes a much longer sequence of bytes than subword tokens, and that makes modeling long-range dependencies more expensive. So I think the question is partly architectural: can we build models that learn useful higher-level representations from bytes without spending the same amount of computation on every byte?

I’m optimistic about that possibility, but I wouldn’t say replacing subword tokenization is inevitable. We need to understand when the flexibility of bytes outweighs the computational cost, especially across different languages.

r001.rationale: The response discusses byte sequences being longer and the need for efficiency, but does not suggest downsampling predictable sequences into fewer processing units than subword models.
